overview.title: What is the LOHAS Five-Line Analysis?
overview.content: The LOHAS five-line chart calculates a trend line from a period of prices, then measures how far the current price sits from that trend line — towards greed or towards fear.
overview.readMore: For detailed instructions, please see the article

sd.title: How do I read a holding’s sentiment?
sd.point1: The middle line is a trend line calculated from the price, showing the long-term direction of the holding. Two standard-deviation lines either side mark how far price strays from that trend. The further price sits from the middle line, the more likely it is to revert towards it — which is what tells you whether the current price sits in greed or in fear.
sd.point2: The LOHAS Channel compares price against the range it has traded in over the last 20 weeks, as a second read on sentiment.
sd.point3: Touching the top line of the five-line chart means "Extreme Greed". Check whether the LOHAS Channel has also broken above its upper edge: when both have, price may be about to weaken; when only the five-line chart has, it has a chance of running a little further.
sd.point4: At Extreme Fear, check whether price is also below the LOHAS Channel. Across 43 index ETFs in this backtest, the median share of entries ending higher after one year was 88% when both conditions held, versus 74% for random entry.

ulband.title: What is the LOHAS Channel?
ulband.point1: The LOHAS Channel builds its edges from the highs and lows of the last 20 weeks, showing whether the current price has moved out of its recent range.
ulband.point2: Price above the upper edge has risen past its price range of the last 20 weeks.
ulband.point3: Price below the lower edge has fallen out of its price range of the last 20 weeks.

tips.title: What kind of holdings is the LOHAS five-line chart suited to?
tips.usage: It is recommended for use with index ETFs or large-cap stocks with clear trends, in conjunction with fundamental analysis.
tips.limitation: It should not be used as the sole basis for a trade, and it carries higher risk when applied to individual stocks.

horizons.title: What is "Other spans"?
horizons.point1: The same holding can read differently across spans. For example, the 0.5-year span may sit at extreme fear while the 3.5-year span shows greed — which reads as: it has fallen hard lately, but on a longer view it has not yet returned to a low.
horizons.point2: When all three spans point the same way, the signal is stronger than any single span: short, medium and long term all show the same extreme.
horizons.point3: When all three horizons show Extreme Fear, check whether price is also below the channel and whether the broad market shows fear too. Together, these conditions help distinguish an isolated correction from a widespread decline.

indicators.title: Other indicators
indicators.body: MA is shown by default, comparing price with 5, 10, 20, 60, and 120-day moving averages. Pro can switch to RSI, MACD, or KD to examine price momentum.

result.title: Analysis results
result.body: The summary shows price, market sentiment, other spans, and channel position. Below it are the LOHAS five-line chart and LOHAS Channel. Compare the two charts to read price sentiment and channel position; the question marks beside the sentiment and channel labels explain how to interpret them.

search.title: Enter a stock code
search.body: Enter a numeric code for Taiwan stocks or a ticker for US stocks, such as 2330 or AAPL. Pick one from the results, or just press Enter, and the analysis starts.

period.title: Adjust the analysis span here
period.body: The default span is 3.5 years; switch to 0.5 or 1.5 years. Choose Custom and enter a span, then press Enter or leave the field to update. Pick a backtest date to see the analysis as of that day.
